mappings.note: Identifies conduction through the pan, convection in the water and radiation felt at a distance in one scene: all three modes of heat transfer.

Ice stupas as a way of storing winter water for a dry spring is conservation of a scarce natural resource. Cited at competency level because LO-94 lists pollutants, tree planting and sanitation, none of which covers water storage.
How the stupa helps is that a large ice mass melts slowly and releases water steadily: the melting behaviour put to practical use. The item that names the practice is on C-SCI4.1.
Body a good conductor, handle a poor one: the conductor-and-insulator-of-heat differentiation named in LO-82.
Predicting that the pins fall nearest-first requires knowing that heat travels progressively along the strip by conduction. Not LO-84, because the experiment is reasoned about, not performed.
Putting a smoke detector on the ceiling because hot smoke rises is the phenomenon applied to a safety decision at home.
Names infiltration as the seeping of surface water into soil and rock, a stage of the water cycle.
Gravel, sand and clay ranked by how fast water passes: three materials separated by a property.
Clay is slowest because its fine particles leave tiny pores: the observed rate traced to its cause. Not LO-82, because the item explains one material rather than ranking them.
Names groundwater as water held in pore spaces underground, a stage in the movement of water.
Names aquifers as the layers that hold and pass groundwater.
Falling groundwater traced to over-extraction and to concrete cutting off recharge, which is the depletion-of-the-water-table-with-human-activities example named verbatim in LO-85.
The bukhari as a wood or charcoal stove with a chimney is a household heating device. Not LO-86, because the item asks what it is, not how it warms the room.
How the bukhari warms a room brings in conduction, convection and radiation together: all three modes at work in one appliance.
Names evaporation, the sun-driven first stage of the water cycle.
Names condensation, where cooled vapour forms cloud droplets.
Names precipitation as rain, snow and hail returning to the ground.
Names the water cycle as the continuous movement of water on, above and below the surface.
How the cycle keeps the supply going by redistributing and replenishing: the process as a whole. Not C-SCI4.1, since no conservation action is asked for.
The one-mark version of the double-tumbler item, trapped air keeping the lassi cold in a practical fix.
Rejects the claim that solids transfer heat by convection because particles cannot flow: the item turns on how each mode works.
Melting ice draws heat from the air and the dish: the change traced to where the heat comes from.
Smoke still rises from a downward-pointing stick because hot gas is less dense: effect tied to cause, with no diagram required here.
Heating from the bottom sets up convection while heating from the top leaves conduction to work slowly downwards: a comparison of how heat moves through water.
Matches dark and light clothing, metal pans and wooden handles to what each does with heat: four everyday applications in one item.
Matches the falling pins, the coloured water, the rising paper cup and the soil-water comparison to their mechanisms, so the item is about the modes of transfer.
Names a material that conducts heat well. A single material identified by a property, so LO-81 rather than LO-83, where the class itself would be named.
Names a material that insulates, the companion identification item.
Names conduction from its description as particle-to-particle transfer without movement.
Conduction as the dominant mode in solids, a statement about how the modes are distributed.
Places air in the poor-conductor class, which is classification by a thermal property.
Heated air expands, becomes lighter and rises: the mechanism that makes convection work.
Names convection from its description as transfer by moving particles.
Picks warmth from sunlight as the one case that is radiation rather than convection, which needs all three modes to be told apart.
Describes conduction along a heated strip in terms of vibrating particles passing energy on: the mechanism in words.
Good against poor conductors with an example of each, the differentiation LO-82 names.
Wool keeps us warm by trapping air, the concept applied to winter clothing.
Two thin blankets over one thick one because of the air layer between them: the same everyday application.
Coastal temperatures stay moderate because water absorbs much heat for little temperature change: a climatic effect traced to a property of water.
Infiltration of rain and snowmelt as the natural recharge of groundwater, a stage of the cycle.
Paper wrapped on a metal rod survives the flame because the metal carries the heat away: the surprising result traced to its cause.
The spiral turns because rising hot air pushes it: another observed effect explained by its cause.
Contrasts conduction and convection on whether the fluid itself flows, a comparison of two modes.
Radiation set apart by needing no medium, the defining difference among the three modes.
